publication.title: Paddle Lab: Make Power Earn Its Place
publication.subtitle: A four-station court check for touch, resets, quick hands, and well-chosen attacks.
publication.format: Original method plus attributed reading note
publication.disclosure: This is a proposed court experiment, not a PointCast hands-on review. Product specifications come from JOOLA; third-party findings are attributed separately.

source_reading_note.title: JohnKew’s findings: two roughness thresholds, with limits
source_reading_note.text: JohnKew’s October 6 newsletter reports that every Tier 1 result in 50 accelerated-wear tests retained at least 33.6 μm Rz and 50.2 μm Rt surface roughness. Tier 1 meant under 5% spin loss after 100 impacts at 70 mph with a 30° paddle angle. These were common thresholds in that dataset, not a sufficient test or universal law; roughness alone does not establish friction. The Power FX earned Tier 3 with 15% spin loss. Its tested 16 mm elongated sample weighed 7.9 oz. The testers described stiffness, loud feedback, quick response, and noticeable off-center vibration, with divided opinions about feel. PointCast’s proposed court card below explores a separate question: how reliably can a player control a paddle through soft shots and selective attacks?
source_reading_note.scope_note: Attributed reporting from the newsletter. The court experiment below is PointCast’s own proposed method; it does not reproduce or validate JohnKew’s lab protocol.

method.title: A paddle demo with a job to do
paragraphs: A good demo should leave you with a clearer decision than “that one felt lively.” PointCast’s Paddle Lab gives each paddle the same four jobs: place a soft ball, absorb pace, recover for the next volley, and attack only when the opening is there. The aim is a repeatable personal comparison. Nobody at PointCast has conducted this test on the Power FX, and the scorecard begins empty. Your entries describe your own session.

Treat the lab-bench theme like a game menu: CONTROL, RESET, HANDS, CHOOSE. Complete all four stations before looking at the total. Keep any favorite sound, color, or brand in a separate notes field so it cannot quietly become an extra point. A satisfying first hit is worth noticing; the rest of the session gives that feeling some context.

method.title: Set the bench before you swing
paragraphs: Bring your familiar paddle, one challenger, a partner, the same set of balls, and a way to mark safe targets outside the playing path. Label the paddles A and B. Record the exact model and thickness, grip setup, any added weight, approximate prior use, and indoor or outdoor conditions. Keep those setups unchanged during the comparison. If one paddle is new and one well used, write that down.

Warm up with both paddles without scoring. Agree on the feed pace and the definition of success at each station. Use ten-shot blocks in the order A, B, B, A, giving each paddle twenty scored attempts per station. Take similar breaks between blocks. On another day, reverse the order. Replay a clearly bad feed before judging the shot, and track replayed feeds so a difficult feeding day remains visible.

method.title: Station 01 · CONTROL
paragraphs: Choose one crosscourt kitchen target large enough to be useful and small enough to demand intention. Keep its position and size fixed for both paddles. Your partner sends comfortable dink feeds, split evenly between forehand and backhand. Count one success when the reply lands in the agreed target and stays below the attackable-height boundary you both chose during warm-up. Count zero for a miss or a ball that meets only one condition.

Log target misses and pop-ups separately, even though either makes the attempt unsuccessful. Those two mistakes suggest different questions for the next session. Were you adjusting the face late? Did shorter swings help? Write observations rather than diagnosing the paddle from twenty balls. The useful comparison is whether the same task became easier to repeat.

method.title: Station 02 · RESET
paragraphs: Stand at a marked transition-zone position. Ask for repeatable, moderate feeds that you can comfortably handle. Try to land a soft reply inside an agreed kitchen target. A success requires both the target landing and the agreed low height. Keep the partner, ball, feed direction, and starting position consistent. Do ten forehand and ten backhand attempts for each paddle across the two blocks.

Add a short note after each block: easy to soften, needed an adjustment, or unpredictable today. Do not turn that feeling into another numeric bonus. The score already counts the outcomes. If you change stance, grip pressure, or swing length halfway through, record the change and try it with both paddles before drawing a conclusion.

method.title: Station 03 · HANDS
paragraphs: At the kitchen line, use controlled alternating forehand and backhand volley feeds. Choose a pace that keeps the drill cooperative. For each scored contact, send the ball into a broad agreed target and recover to a ready position before the next feed. Your partner calls success only when both happen. Keep the feed rhythm fixed, with a fresh start after each missed ball.

The number records your ability to complete this particular task with this setup. It does not measure swing weight, reaction time, or a manufacturer’s hand-speed claim. Note whether misses cluster on one side or late in a block. If fatigue or feeding changes noticeably, pause and repeat the affected block after a comparable rest for each paddle.

method.title: Station 04 · CHOOSE
paragraphs: Have your partner mix ten comfortable attack opportunities with ten lower or awkward balls in a shuffled order for each paddle. Before starting, agree that a balanced, clearly attackable ball invites a controlled attack to a broad target; the other feed calls for a reset to the kitchen target. Make the attack lane safely away from your partner’s face and body.

A successful attempt needs the appropriate choice and the agreed target. A hard shot on the wrong feed scores zero even if it lands in. A sensible reset that misses also scores zero. Mark those as separate errors: choice and execution. If the feed is ambiguous, replay it rather than inventing a verdict. This station rewards selective aggression while still making room for the quiet, correct shot.

method.title: Read the four lines before the total
paragraphs: Enter each success count from zero to twenty. The default control-first weighting is 30 points for CONTROL, 35 for RESET, 20 for HANDS, and 15 for CHOOSE. Divide each count by twenty and multiply by its weight, then add the four contributions. These are PointCast’s proposed preference weights. They are not validated performance standards, league ratings, or John Kew’s scoring system.

Keep the raw counts beside the total. A small gap may come from a couple of feeds, a better warm-up, or ordinary day-to-day variation. Repeat the session before treating it as a reliable difference. If you use different weights, choose them before seeing the results and retain the original counts. There is no universal passing score or automatic buy recommendation.

method.title: Save one question for next time
paragraphs: Finish with three lines: what became easier, what became harder, and what still needs another session. Keep sound and feel alongside the results without presenting them as measured power or durability. You can also track the same paddle at later sessions using the same drill setup, while noting changes in balls, conditions, and technique. A home court log cannot assign a laboratory spin-durability tier.

The useful ending might be “try again,” “keep the familiar paddle,” or “the challenger deserves more time.” Leave a decision open when the evidence is mixed. A good scorecard earns its place by helping you notice a trade-off you otherwise would have missed.

interactive_court_card.title: Your Court Card
interactive_court_card.empty_state: No session recorded. Add your own counts, or load the clearly fictional example.

validation.error: Use a whole number from 0 to 20 for every station.

demo.label: Fictional example only. These numbers are invented and describe no product or actual player.
demo.explanation: Fictional A leads by 0.50 points with the default weights; the raw counts show the trade-off. This is a calculator demonstration, not evidence that a paddle is better.

interactive_court_card.storage: Keep session inputs in current-tab memory only. No server submission, analytics events containing entries, or automatic browser persistence.
accessibility: Visible labels and instructions for every input.
Errors tied to their fields and announced accessibly.
Do not rely on color alone; pair every meter with raw counts and text.
Disable or reduce decorative motion for reduced-motion preferences.
interactive_court_card.score_interpretation: A repeatable personal comparison under these drill conditions. No performance percentile, clinical inference, lab certification, or automatic purchase verdict.

design.description: Four chunky station cards with small original pixel court marks, a cream score slip, dark ink, teal accents, and a warm signal color. Use generic pixel geometry, not Nintendo marks, game sprites, JOOLA artwork, John Kew charts, or copied brand assets.
design.composition: Place the attributed reading note and official product card above the original method. Pin the interactive court card after the four stations, with raw counts as prominent as the total.
design.mobile: Stack cards and keep all inputs at comfortable touch size. Do not require horizontal scrolling.
design.print: Print the procedure, two empty four-station tally cards, conditions, and three closing questions; remove decorative backgrounds.
